“Self-sustaining” here means not depending on another. In the case of a substance, “standing in itself” should also be understood in this implied sense; taking it literally would suggest two things.

Here “knowledge” is the predicate in meaning, and “immaterial existence” is the subject. The argument is: intellect is immaterial existence; every immaterial existence is knowledge; therefore intellect is knowledge. The terms are arranged this way to avoid an invalid inference from two affirmative premises.

This existence—and indeed all existence—is self-evident and makes other things evident, so it is light. Because it acts knowingly and willingly, it is powerful; because it perceives and acts, it is living. The other perfections of the simple, necessary being are drawn from the one reality of His essence.

This means that the two sides differ only in the figurative relations described above, and that the difference between them occurs within the relation itself. But that is not the apparent meaning of the quoted scholar’s words, which seem to claim a real difference.

The quoted passage does not cover every kind of individuation. In God, individuality is not additional to reality. Nor, when a kind exists in only one individual, does its essence cause its individuation; an essence does not cause anything, unless “cause” means only that nothing else causes it. The author’s next claim—that being a knower or known is a feature of existence, not of essence—is aimed at the quoted account. That account seems to be attributed to Avicenna as a way to explain phrases like “my self” and “your self,” not to explain how an immaterial being knows itself. The latter explanation appears to be the quoted writer’s own addition; this is supported by the reliable reading of The Healing and The Pointers.

“Some” excludes relations such as possession and action, which are included in “and other features.” The five features listed share this point: the specific instances of them can vary, but their general kinds remain. For example, colors, tastes, and smells can change, but some quality remains; the same is true of shape, touch, and other features. Time is shared in general, but the particular way each thing occupies time is its own.

By “individual,” the author means a natural particular in sense or imagination, not a particular meaning. He insists on this view in several of his books, including the section on the soul in this work and The Keys to the Unseen. I find this claim puzzling as stated. Love, hatred, and similar states occur in many individuals, as different animals have different appetites and at different times. Time and the features surrounding a soul also help make such states particular. There are particular meanings of love, desire, and will, yet the intellect does not grasp particular meanings, and neither does sense or imagination. Perhaps the author means a mistaken estimate, since falsehood and evil are not independent realities. He often keeps divine unity in view. The author may say that in animals, these states are perceived by the intellects that govern their kinds, rather than by our intellect. The traditions explain unusual animal perceptions as angelic inspiration, or, in the Illuminationist view, as contact with the lord of the kind.

Estimation does not grasp every intellectual form tied to an individual, such as human, horse, black, or white. It grasps particular inner states such as love, hatred, joy, and sorrow. The common sense may perceive these, as the author will explain in the section on the soul. Calling them “meanings,” as opposed to forms perceived by the outer senses, does not make them a different kind of act that requires a separate faculty. The better view is to set aside estimation as a distinct faculty and assign its work to the common sense.

The commentator counts sensation, imagination, and intellect as the real kinds, setting aside estimation just as he sets aside sensation as a separate kind. The fact that matter is present or absent does not make the perceived thing different, though the form is usually clearer to the soul when the matter is present; sometimes an imagined form, through the soul’s attention, is even clearer.

In this respect, the intellect has an angelic role, like Azrael. By reviving ignorant souls through teaching, it also has a role like Israfil or Gabriel. The human being is a comprehensive whole containing all these roles.

The common explanation mistakenly treats universality as a feature of the object known, and only indirectly of the act of knowledge. The correct account treats knowledge as universal in itself, while the known thing is universal only indirectly. Knowledge is luminous existence: it is wide-ranging, simple, and all-embracing.
The universal humanity applies to many people; the humanity in each one does not.

The universal humanity is not the humanity found in two people together, or in all people as one collective whole. The humanity in one person is not identical with the two-person whole. A better reply would ask whether the universal known exists outside the mind. If it is the universal in individuals, or a collective whole, the same objection defeats it. If it is an essence considered in itself, it is not universal. If it exists in the mind but is distinct from the mind, as al-Qūshjī argues, it is refuted by the earlier discussion of mental existence.

Defining universality as “applying to many” raises problems, so philosophers shifted to defining it as “being shared.” Since that definition also has difficulties, they explain sharing this way: when the universal exists in matter, it is the individuals; when those individuals are understood, they are the universal.

The point is that this all-embracing existence is universal and shared because it contains its individual instances and is equally related to them. Its intellectual individuality does not conflict with this reach.

If the soul’s ordinary subject and its surrounding features remained in place, they would make the intellectual image particular. But understanding is the knower becoming one with what it knows, so the knower changes into it. To truly reach a meaning, the soul must become it and pass away into it. This does not mean that the soul simply disappears: its unity is not numerical or limited, but a true, dependent unity. When it changes in one respect, it remains in its other aspects. This change happens in the potential intellect, not in the soul’s imaginative level, where it already has actual particular images. The potential intellect has many levels, like prime matter. When prime matter becomes fire, for example, it can also become air or a human being; one change does not rule out its receiving other forms.

The author does not say that its relation to individuals is equal, because the universal intellect does not depend on individuals; when it exists, they are not yet there. Individuals, by contrast, depend on it and must be related to it.

Abstraction does not mean that the soul stays in its own intellectual place while images move from matter through sense and imagination to intellect. Rather, the soul rises and joins, indeed becomes one with, the Active Intellect and its perceptions after leaving behind the sensory and imaginal modes.
“Becoming one” here means actual realization, not merely being related to something or thinking about it. It is an existence that becomes the thing, not just knowledge or thought about it.

For example, if you know the reality of the heavens—their broader kinds, defining features, external matter and bodily form, natural powers, individual soul, and universal soul, as far as a human being can—you have gathered that reality into your own being. This is more complete than merely having a sense image of the heavens.
In the same way, if the features of existence—that is, the essences—are set aside, one underlying reality remains.

The commentator says it would be more accurate to say that giving intellectual things bodily images is the work of imagination, not intellect. That description confuses the faculties. The intellect truly distinguishes one into many, because it can understand simplicity through proof; imagination pictures it as a point. The intellect understands true light, while imagination pictures sunlight. The intellect understands all-embracing reality, while imagination pictures spatial extension. Still, “multiplying one” can mean either the mistaken imagining described above or a proper act of intellect: distinguishing different aspects, names, and attributes of God, or distinguishing the levels of existence from simple beings up through plants, animals, and human beings.

The soul’s potential to understand is counted as a kind of understanding because a thing’s potential is its first trace: without it, the thing could not exist or rise from a lower state to a higher one. Avicenna does not specify this potential stage; instead, he divides acquired knowledge into two kinds, as the author explains below.
Even the potential intellect’s knowledge of itself is only potential. It might merely imagine itself, as an ignorant soul does, or imagine itself as something with a position and face.

The second kind means detailed intelligible forms held in the intellect. It is the first of Avicenna’s three kinds, but because imagination helps arrange those forms in sequence, he says they are held in an imaginative power. He may instead mean an intellectual power mixed with or related to imagination.

This objection confuses intellect with imagination and rejects a general truth because it is absent in one particular case. Because a person cannot find the forms in imagination, they assume they cannot be in intellect—as though the soul were nothing but imagination. They wrongly assume that because the forms are not present as many, they cannot be present as one. Avicenna and other careful thinkers should not call this state potential knowledge while a person is eating or drinking; they should call it strong knowledge. The soul has faculties of sense, imagination, estimation, detailed intellect, and simple intellect. Four may not be perceiving, while the fifth still knows. This is especially true when the person is almost pure intellect and the partial faculties have been brought into line with it. Notice that such a person need not acquire anything new through effort. Simple intellect is a manifestation of the One who is not distracted by one affair from another. True speech is grasping universals and communicating with immaterial beings. A prophetic report says that among the community are people who receive direct insight. This is one way of reading the revealed Book in a single timeless act. This intellect belongs to the world of pure intellect and timelessness, even if its outward form is in the natural world and it still uses bodily faculties. Its higher activity does not keep it from ordinary activity. A person with firm spiritual grounding sees particulars as mirrors of universals, not the other way around. Anyone who rejects this sees the body, or the soul merely as soul, as the self—and so fails to see that self’s higher capacity. “Knowledge of your soul is no trivial matter; if you know it truly, you know what it is.”
This means knowledge either unfolded in detail, or knowledge held more strongly.

A fact cannot be established for something unless that thing exists. When the speaker says, “This is present in me,” the word “this” points intellectually to something that exists in act. In either reading, the answer to the question is already known in act.
This refers to the way intellectual forms exist for separate beings in simple intellect, not to material forms or images that belong to the soul’s own psychic world.

The union must preserve simplicity. If the knower existed through one existence and each intelligible through a separate existence, however closely connected, they would make a composite whole. Simplicity is preserved only if all exist through one existence and multiplicity belongs to the meanings understood.

Someone might say that the Active Intellect is usually taken to be the storehouse of intelligibles, and that in every act of knowing our partial intellect connects with or faces it. How, then, can Avicenna call simple intellect the storehouse, especially before knowledge has become a settled habit? There is no conflict if, as explained earlier, the horse understood by the Active Intellect and the horse understood by a thousand intellects is one. Avicenna’s account works only if intellect and intelligible are one, though he rejects that view. His position is inconsistent.

“Intelligibles” here means intelligibles in themselves, in detail; “things” means things known indirectly, that is, external things. The essences are one in both, but existence differs in strength, weakness, completeness, and incompleteness. The differences between levels of existence are not differences between wholly unrelated realities.

The commentator says “what follows from His attributes” means the essences that follow from God’s attributes. Their existence is contained in the existence of those attributes, which is itself contained in God’s existence. Their meanings are not later in existence, as a geometrical body follows from a natural body, or measured time from successive motion. Unity and individuality also follow from certain kinds of real existence. Or the phrase may mean the effects that follow from God’s acts: the existence of the cause is the higher form of existence for its effects. A thing is fully itself, not in a diminished way; and the stronger its existence, the more it contains meanings. Stronger light reveals more essences, and knowledge of the cause entails knowledge of its effect.

I grant that the form, which makes a thing actual, is one. If by “form” we mean a single essence, it cannot represent many different essences. But if it means one existence, united in a true unity and infinitely intense in its light, it can reveal all existences and contain many meanings and essences. As the saying goes, “God’s hand is with the gathering.” The same is true of the human simple intellect: its existence is one and powerful, yet it is one with the many essences that appear distinctly in detailed thought. All these essences exist in it as meanings, while their existence is one. If we look at their one existence, we see how one act of knowledge can know many, even countless, things. If we look at the many essences contained in simple intellect, we see how many acts of knowledge can be present together. But remember that the knower in both cases is pure intellect, not the soul’s detailed understanding and certainly not imagination. “You are too great to appear in a small mirror.” If someone imagines that neither kind of knowledge is actually present in simple intellect, they are mistaking themselves for imagination or ordinary understanding. As the verse says, “As long as you imagine yourself confined to a before and an after, you are bound to the body and deprived of the soul.” In God, detail exists within an all-at-once knowledge, and unity within detailed knowledge: the many known things are one in the act of knowing. Knowledge and its object are one, though—as with existence and essence—they differ in how we conceive them. This avoids the two objections raised by the critic.

The commentator asks how someone who does not know the real nature of the answers can be sure that all the answers are present or that they will address the questions. Any answer does not fit any question. By contrast, we can know that something moves the body without knowing what it is, because we know one aspect of it while other aspects remain unknown. Whether the soul is a nature, a bodily mixture, or immaterial, it can move the body.

In this respect, simple intellect manifests the divine names of the One whom no thing hides from another and whom no affair distracts from another. Even the common sense gathers five kinds of sensation in one moment: sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste. While seeing, we may also hear, feel the air’s temperature, smell, and taste. The common sense is then aware of five worlds at once. When it senses something while awake and imagination combines or separates images that it presents at the same time, there are at least two acts of perception; with the perception of particular meanings, the soul has three. So what should we expect of intellect, especially simple intellect? The endless number of intelligibles is also clear. One general claim, such as “Everything that comes to be will pass away,” branches into countless claims about animals, plants, minerals, incomplete compounds, particular animals, and countless land and sea creatures. The same applies to relations, opposites, and other general truths. These unrecorded examples point to countless other propositions and concepts, all intelligible as one simple reality to the true intellectual human being, in one timeless act.
The wording is loose. “Several acts of knowledge in one moment” means that they are grasped together, without a sequence. Immaterial knowledge is not itself measured by time or by a moment.

This explanation does not fully answer the objection. The author elsewhere treats imagination as immaterial like intellect, so why can it not hold all its images together without sequence? Two things may explain the limit. First, the imaginative powers have material organs in the body—eyes, ears, and parts of the brain—that perform material operations and prepare the soul for particular perceptions. The resistance comes from these bodily powers, not from the immaterial psychic power itself. Second, even if imagination is free of matter, it still has some features of matter, such as quantity and certain qualities. This makes its images occur in an order, and ordered parts cannot all be present together. If we imagine dawn, then sunrise, noon, sunset, and darkness, each stage naturally gives way to the next, even though the whole image is free of matter.

We have also shown that sense can gather several perceptions at once. The chapter would therefore have been better titled “Whether the soul can have many kinds of knowledge at once,” since the examples include several sensations, imagination, estimation, detailed understanding, and simple understanding together.

You may ask whether understanding is an action or a passive reception, since the soul acts on the body but receives from the immaterial world above it. There are two answers. First, this develops the idea of simple intellect, which the philosophers also distinguish from detailed knowledge. Second, the author treats the grasp of particular things, such as imagined forms, as the soul’s active creation. The soul is active in producing the many, changing images of detailed knowledge.

This includes the soul’s life, power, and knowledge of itself: immediate knowledge in which the soul is present to itself, without further divisions. Knowledge can also be divided into acquired and direct knowledge. Direct knowledge includes an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself, a thing’s direct awareness of its effect, and the awareness of a person who has become one with what they know. Knowledge can be general or exact, and general or detailed. The author’s example of human knowledge needs to be read in reverse, as the context makes clear.

The prophet’s true self and inner heart connect with the Active Intellect and, through it, with all the separate intellects in the ascending order. The prophet receives direct spiritual teaching and learns the simple realities of things. A saint may connect with the finer, lower-level aspect of the Active Intellect—the one most suited to the people of their time—and receive its images and spoken words. For the friends of God, sages, and those who know God, a complete union of their true selves with the true self of the intellect is rare. Each person is enabled for what they were made to do.

The issue is not an endless chain of teachers across different people and times. It is whether one person’s thought about a single subject depends on earlier thought from a teacher without end. If every step in one person’s reasoning had to be taught, the chain would never reach the self-evident ideas from which reasoning begins. For example, the idea of a human being may be learned from the ideas of animal and rational; those from substance, able to have dimensions, living, sensing, and understanding; and those from ideas such as existence and possibility. At the root, the thinker knows existence, possibility, increase, perception, and knowledge for themselves. This is what philosophers mean when they say that the chain of concepts cannot continue forever.

Knowing that the Active Intellect is immaterial in both its being and its action, has no unrealized potential, completes souls, and is the storehouse and source of their intelligible forms is not the heart of direct knowledge. The heart of it is becoming and being transformed by that reality. General knowledge is still a means to this direct encounter when its meanings become firm in the soul. “Knowledge is the seed of direct vision.” May God help us join knowledge with action and protect us from error, through Muhammad and his family, the friends of God who reach the universal intellects and rise beyond them.

The argument for both claims can be summarized this way. For the first: if a cause is a cause through its full causal reality, then knowing it means knowing its necessary effect. The known cause and effect must be present together in knowledge. If the cause acts through its existence, then direct knowledge of that existence is together with the existence of its effect, since the effect’s existence depends on it. Merely knowing the cause’s essence does not reveal the effect, because causality belongs to existence, not essence. For the second claim: if the effect follows from an essence, knowing it gives knowledge of some cause, since the effect may follow from a broader essence. If it follows from existence, direct knowledge of its existence gives knowledge of an aspect of its cause, but not complete knowledge of the cause. The effect’s essence alone does not establish any cause.

This premise is the heart of the argument: the cause and effect are known together. It does not say that knowledge of the cause is a prior cause of knowledge of the effect, as al-Rāzī objects. Saying that the cause’s existence includes the relational existence of its effect does not remove the fact that they are known together. The best reading is that the author means a direct, illuminating relation between them, if this fits the philosophers’ words.

Knowledge of real existence cannot be merely a mental copy; it must be direct. Direct knowledge has three cases: an immaterial being’s knowledge of itself, its knowledge of its effect, and a thing’s knowledge of what it has become one with. The author’s claim seems to apply this rule specifically to direct knowledge of existence, as is correct in his view. Other philosophers do not limit it this way. For example, they say that knowledge of a barrier causes knowledge of a hollow, or knowledge of an opposing angle causes knowledge of a crescent shape. Those are not cases of direct knowledge. For them, God’s knowledge of Himself is direct, but His knowledge of effects is acquired through images in His being. The author does not always restrict his rule to direct knowledge; here, his wording “in its real identity” points to that restriction.
This objection also fails when a thing has no essence separate from existence.

The philosophers say both that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect and that the reverse does not follow. But if cause and effect are known together simply because they are correlatives, the same should hold in both directions. Also, their question concerns knowing a particular cause and effect, not the broad concepts of cause and effect.
The objection also reverses: knowing every aspect of an effect would include knowing that it follows from a particular cause.
This word should be read as “all the aspects,” not “if,” since it continues the reasoning and does not begin a new condition.
Someone might reply that the argument is about what we need in order to prove something, not what makes it exist. But knowing the part is also part of knowing the whole.
There is no need to answer the condition separately; this sentence explains what the philosophers mean by saying that knowing the cause means knowing the effect.

The author’s reply does not fully solve the second part of the objection: that related things are known together in thought and in the outside world, while he claims knowledge of the cause comes before knowledge of the effect. His reply also seems to accept that the category of relation is added to God’s being. A better answer is that the effect is a feature of the cause’s existence and depends on it, so the cause’s existence cannot be present in full without containing its effect. Direct knowledge of the cause therefore gives direct knowledge of the effect. The category of relation applies to the concepts of cause and effect, not to their existence.

This is like an attribute’s existence. It is one simple existence outside the mind. When related to its broad kind, such as color, it exists as a feature and depends on that kind. When related to its distinguishing feature, such as the way it separates light from the eye, it is also a cause, since the distinguishing feature gives the broad kind its specific form.

Even those who say that relations do not exist in their own separate right need not say they do not exist at all. A relation exists through the thing that gives rise to it. The argument against a separate existence for relations only rules out that first sense.

An essential property, such as evenness, differs from the essence in both its meaning and its existence in the mind. Four is a quantity; evenness is a feature of quantity. The author likely means only that the effect necessarily follows from the cause, not that it has the same kind of existence. His discussion may also apply only to causes and effects in divine philosophy.

“Full understanding” means that the mind’s account matches reality. In direct knowledge, it becomes one with that reality. The question may be intended to challenge this full union. Otherwise, there is no point in the argument: a complete cause cannot fail to produce its effect. Philosophers who discuss God’s knowledge of other things all agree that the effect is present in knowledge of the cause, though they differ on whether this is direct knowledge of existence, a mental form, luminous images, or timeless essences. A cause and effect can differ, yet the effect is present when the cause is present, just as evenness is present when four is understood. The point is not to reject full knowledge.
This point applies only to direct knowledge. The previous argument used it in that sense.

An effect cannot be particular before the cause makes it particular. Its individual identity comes from the cause. Some philosophers say that certain kinds, such as immaterial beings, cause their own individual identity. The commentator rejects this: no essence can produce individuation, because individuality belongs to existence. A particular existence gives the essence its individual identity. A particular defining feature likewise makes the broad kind into a particular species. Al-Rāzī misses this point when he assumes that a broad kind such as body already exists on its own and then asks what makes it one particular type.

This is a claim made in the logical book The Demonstration: certainty about something that has a cause can come only through certainty about its cause. Certainty is knowledge that something is so and cannot be otherwise. If we know that an effect exists, then we must already know that its cause exists; otherwise the effect could exist without its cause. Philosophers use this rule to set aside one kind of proof from effects: reasoning from an effect back to its own cause. They accept two kinds of proof: one that starts from a cause and establishes its effect, and one that reasons from general signs of an effect to signs of another effect. Later notes explain the limits of this claim.

Some philosophers say that all caused things can be known only through their causes. The problem is that this seems to rule out immediate knowledge, such as seeing. The commentator says the rule should not be weakened. The existence of every effect depends on its cause, and every possible thing depends on God. The mind first knows a cause’s existence and then the existence of its effect. As ʿAlī is reported to have said, “I never saw a thing without seeing God before it.”

“Matches” here means is one with. The intellectual form is the real existence itself in direct knowledge; in acquired knowledge, it is the form known directly. It may also mean that what the mind considers matches reality. In reality, each thing depends on God, so the intellect sees it that way. Being one with what is known also brings a kind of union with the known thing indirectly, since the essence appears in the mind and existence follows the same kind of existence.

This was explained earlier in the discussion of how things are brought into existence. A cause and effect share the same kind of existence: a cause of existence must itself be existence, and a cause of essence must be essence. Existence is primary in reality. If it were only an idea drawn from things, it could not belong to the highest reality. Knowing an effect that exists would then reveal its cause. If existence were only an idea, its reality would be the essence from which it is drawn.

This rule also applies to essence. We know an essence through the parts that make it what it is, such as its broad kind and distinguishing feature. These are causes that make up the essence, not causes that bring it into existence.
Particular existence is what removes nonexistence. It is the answer to both “what is it?” and “does it exist?”
Existence as existence does not change. Change belongs to the world as a set of objects, not to existence itself. God’s knowledge does not change.
Otherwise, there would be a third, independent cause that gives us knowledge of the effect apart from the cause that gives the effect its existence.

A relation is like a form, while its two sides are like the matter that receives it; both sides are needed before the relation can be known. This is still knowledge through the cause. A building displays the builder, and a book displays its author. As something received by matter, the building is an effect; as an expression of its maker, it reveals its cause first and itself second.

For example, people may be certain that everyone dies, yet their certainty can fade if someone argues that a natural compound might last forever. Those who know the causes of decay—each compound’s parts tend toward their natural places, its powers are limited, and forced states do not last—cannot lose their certainty that natural compounds will break down. Anyone who says this is only knowledge from experience, not from causes, is mistaken. Experiments help the knower see the cause’s particular features.
The first claim—that knowing the cause gives knowledge of the effect—is subtle; the second claim—that knowledge of an effect cannot reveal its particular cause—is even more subtle.

This is a list where one or more cases must apply, but they need not all apply. The three kinds of knowledge all occur in relation to the Necessary Being: knowing the concept, knowing the full reality, and knowing that it exists. The same three distinctions apply to existence.
God’s essence has no definition, but the meanings of His attributes can be defined and supported by proof.
This refers to the level of pure unity, to existence extended through all things, and to every essence and every limited existence. It also includes the ranks through which beings descend and rise.

The commentator says the author, who manifested God’s names of knowledge, wisdom, and power, knew that words could not express the answer. The question requires three principles. First, the existence of a cause makes up the existence of its effect: the effect’s appearance is contained in the cause’s appearance. Second, true bringing-into-existence is the real, all-pervading existence that flows from God; as explained earlier, this flow has one source. This existence, when related to God, is His act of bringing things into being; when related to created things, it is their existence. Third, God’s creative power has levels. The highest is His direct causation of the intellects; the intellects act through His power, and this power reaches down through the levels of nature. All are expressions of His power.

With these points in view, a person’s reliable knowledge of themselves comes after reliable knowledge of their source, but only through the source’s illuminating presence and creative act. The cause’s existence makes up the effect’s existence. Knowledge works in the same way: knowledge of the source is its own existence, while knowledge of the self is the effect’s existence. Since the relation between source and effect is one of bringing into being, our knowledge of the source is its existence as it causes us. This knowledge comes before knowledge of ourselves, because the source brings us into being.

The commentator adds a second answer: if knowing oneself is identical with one’s own existence, then God’s existence cannot remain beside it as a separate object of knowledge. Knowing God’s existence is His existence, just as knowing ourselves is our existence.

He offers a third answer for a more ordinary reader. The claim “knowing ourselves is identical with our being” does not by itself prove that our knowledge is strong or certain; even an animal has immediate awareness of itself, and people who have forgotten God may still know themselves. Direct knowledge has levels: the soul as sensing, imagining, estimating, or thinking, and the simple intellect of a complete person. Knowledge of oneself through simple intellect is stronger than the ordinary forms of direct awareness. The author’s reply continues from the claim that God has no cause or definition to explain how a complete person can know God through the highest form of direct presence.

The main reason philosophers defend this account is to preserve the priority of knowledge: a freely chosen act must be preceded by knowledge and will. In the Illuminationist view, knowledge does not come before the act; it is the act itself. These philosophers seem to posit an intermediate realm between God’s simple, necessary existence and contingent beings: divine knowledge, containing the forms of all things, from the highest pearl to the smallest speck. These forms are grounded in God, not derived from things, so His knowledge is not passive. The Sufis describe a similar intermediate realm as the level of unity, the world of names and attributes and their fixed realities.
The author has already shown that God is necessary in every respect, including in His acts. His attributes must therefore also be necessary: He necessarily knows, has power, wills, and so on.
This raises two further problems: God would be moving toward greater perfection, and He would be affected by something outside Himself. Every accidental feature depends on a cause.

Natural kinds exist, and the universal nature exists in them, much as the continuous motion that traces a path exists through its successive parts. Creation first brings kinds into existence; they are originated directly and do not need an intermediary to connect them with the eternal.
“Eclipse” here means a lunar eclipse, as shown by the reference to the moon moving from it toward an opposite position.

Avicenna’s main concern is to show that God’s knowledge does not change with the changing existence of things, which would also make His knowledge follow rather than precede His acts. Nor does He know them through images taken from the things themselves, which would make His knowledge passive. He knows them through forms that flow from the principles and causes before the things arise. These forms are specified so that each one points to a single individual. Their role is like a mirror through which that individual is revealed. The individual is known as an individual, even though its form is intellectual. A thing may have many distinguishable features and still be one individual. The author has also said that a bodily form is known through an imagined or luminous intellectual form. These causal forms are far more complete than the things they cause and contain their perfections. Their presence in God therefore reveals the full particulars. Philosophers agree that God knows particulars, though they explain this in different ways. Avicenna’s point is not that particulars disappear from divine knowledge: intellectual knowledge does not rule out particularity. Since no concern distracts God from another, He knows each particular together with all others. The Aristotle’s followers aim to show that God’s knowledge is stable, prior, and active; they hold that this requires forms proceeding from the cause. The doctrine that the simple reality is all things in a higher way can explain this more fully, but the point remains that Avicenna did not deny any form of divine knowledge.

The passage seems to admit that the image in knowledge changes when a material particular changes, which would conflict with the claim that even sensory and imagined knowledge is immaterial. The commentator’s answer is that the images themselves do not change. What changes is their appearance to the soul, which depends on bodily acts such as seeing and hearing. When those acts stop, the image is no longer present to awareness, but the image itself remains; otherwise, we could not recall an earlier sensory image as the very one we once perceived. Knowing change, motion, or divisible quantity does not make knowledge itself change, move, or divide. A mental image must match the external thing in essence, not in its mode of existence.

The argument assumes that the direct object of knowledge is the same at both times, since the opponent treats the two acts of knowledge as one. Any difference would belong only to the indirect object—the day and night outside the mind. When night arrives, the knowledge must remain one if the claim is true. This restates the problem the argument is meant to expose.

This distinction may refer to individual motions of the outermost sphere, which mark time, and to other motions that occur in time. Strictly speaking, even the outermost sphere moves in time. The terms “in” and “with” can be used in different ways: time may be in motion as an accident is in its subject, while motion is in time as something measured is in its measure. The measured thing and its measure are linked. Something may also exist alongside time without motion, as philosophers say of bodily substances. Something “in time” is measured by the flow of the sphere’s motion. What has no motion is not in time by its nature, unless it exists only instantaneously.
The first kind is bodies; the second is bodily things or states.
“Position” here means the arrangement and relation of parts, as a category. The earlier sense is what allows something to be pointed out by the senses.

One might object that this philosopher considers space to be an immaterial dimension. If space is a surface, its material character is clear; if it is a dimension, it is material because it is the place occupied by matter. Or the point may simply be that anything tied to time and space is material.

The Illuminationists and this philosopher deny prime matter, but even those who accept it do not regard it as sheer nonexistence. The same is even clearer of bodily extension. When the author calls matter a source of absence, he means that it is not fully present to itself: each part is hidden from every other part, and the whole is not present to each part. But this is not absence in the strict sense, where a negative statement has no existing subject. Matter has an intermediate mode of existence, between nonexistence and a complete, unified existence. A bodily kind or natural form has a fuller existence than matter. Since these are all modes of existence, they are also kinds of knowledge by virtue of existence; they can be present to a knower. Existence, at every level, is light, whether dim or bright. Even a shadow is a kind of light mixed with darkness. At every level, an existent being is present to its source more fully than its existence is present to itself. That forms exist in matter does not prevent their presence to the all-encompassing source. Our knowledge, by contrast, depends on images because our relation of knowledge is not joined to the relation of bringing things into being.

The commentator asks who claims that a sensible thing itself becomes intelligible: it remains sensible, though it is known without a bodily tool. A philosopher such as Suhrawardī, who says God is seeing and hearing and that His knowledge is presence rather than a form, should not hesitate to say that these particulars are directly perceived by God.

The philosopher does not mean a categorical relation, but an illuminating relation. The great philosophers say that contingent, changing things are possible and changing in themselves, yet necessary and perfectly stable in relation to God. As existences and manifestations of God, they are necessary and stable. Ancient thinkers also held that times and places are like a single instant or point when seen from higher principles, especially from the First Principle. They illustrate this with a colored thread stretched before a person while an ant walks along it. Dāmād says that successive events in time coexist in the container of eternity, like troops passing one after another through a mountain pass as seen by a person watching from above. To grasp this, compare seeing one white thing with imagining it, then with understanding “every white thing” and making a universal judgment about all of them. The intellect encompasses them all, each according to its capacity. The author says that disappearing from or being absent to some beings does not mean being absent to others. Things with positions are so only in relation to one another, not in relation to separate intellects. Although the author does not explicitly mention existence or its primacy here, elsewhere he rejects the view that knowledge is merely a relation and speaks of the “book of existence.” This shows that he treats existence as real.

No one means that a material thing ceases to be material when considered by higher principles. Rather, relative to a separate intellect, matter is as if stripped of matter; likewise, place and time are as if stripped of place and time, because they are no longer hidden from the knower. The author elsewhere reports Dāmād’s warning not to mistake this kind of language for a denial of the material world.

The example is not literally possible, since the outermost sphere does not truly surround everything. A better example would be a sight that extends through the greatest sphere and all within it, just as existence and necessity extend through everything. From that standpoint, nothing is near or far.

This is general knowledge that includes detailed disclosure: each cause contains all the existences below it in a higher way. It is general because the higher existence is one and simple; it is detailed because that one is the very reality of the many. A thing is what it is in its full reality, not through what it lacks. Individuality and distinction belong to existence, while the essences of these existences follow from it without being later in existence. More tentatively, the Aristotle’s followers may mean by forms in causes the existences of their effects enfolded within them.

Anyone who says that all knowledge of other things is not limited to mental forms must accept that a cause knows its effect directly. How, then, can perception be limited to forms? Knowledge through a form is only needed when the knower is not the cause of what is known. Those who say all knowledge of other things is acquired knowledge through forms are the ones who must limit perception to forms.

That applies to acquired knowledge. Direct knowledge depends on the cause’s mastery and its illuminating relation to the effect, as explained in the commentary on The Pointers. The forms that arise from a knower are known directly and do not need further forms to reveal them. Pure existence contains all that belongs to its kind and lacks what is alien to it; nonexistence is what is alien to existence. For the Illuminationists, a thing’s being light to itself and to others is the same kind of principle.
“That exists” describes “form”; “to be” may be a complete verb or a linking verb, depending on the reading.
That is, whatever way it is taken to exist, absent or present. The point is that material existence alone would be enough for a relation of knowledge; no mental form would be needed.
